suggestions: State the lineup size (~116 funds) and that the catalog is refreshed from a page cached for 24 h, so an agent knows both the scan cost and the staleness bound.

Name the two tables' join key explicitly at catalog level (`products.ticker` = `holdings.fund_ticker`), since the two columns have different names and an agent reading only the catalog doc will guess `ticker` = `ticker`.
Add the coverage boundary that is invisible from the structure: US-listed Global X ETFs only, no NAV history, no historical holdings, no ISIN/CUSIP.
3149b6d7ed2a2683.summary: Accurate, well-pitched catalog framing; only misses scale, staleness, and the differently-named join key.

suggestions: The schema doc is nearly a restatement of the catalog doc — differentiate it by naming the objects' relationship concretely (one row per fund in `products`; many rows per fund in `holdings`, joined `products.ticker = holdings.fund_ticker`).
Mention that `holdings` is hive-partitioned and that an unfiltered scan fans out over every fund, since that is the single biggest cost decision an agent makes at this level.
Say that some funds have no published holdings file and are silently absent from `holdings`, so a `products` ticker is not guaranteed to have holdings rows.
d7fc4d95d49c2ac1.summary: Clear and accurate but largely duplicates the catalog doc without adding the join, partitioning, or coverage facts an agent needs here.

suggestions: "Rows come back weight-descending" in doc_llm overstates the contract — the scan emits weight-descending per partition, but SQL gives no ordering guarantee across partitions or after any operator. Reword to "rows are emitted weight-descending within each fund; add ORDER BY weight_percent DESC if you depend on it" (the examples already do).
ee8eb2ea7c28c51b.summary: Strong, agent-oriented docs; the implied ordering guarantee and the unmentioned composite primary key are the two gaps.

suggestions: `net_expense_ratio_percent`'s comment says "null when equal to gross", but the driver nulls it whenever the source field is absent (`$undefined`) — which is not the same claim. Say "null when Global X does not publish a separate net ratio (typically when it equals gross)" so an agent does not COALESCE on a false invariant.

Note that the return columns are null for funds younger than the window (`return_10y_percent` is null for most of the lineup) and that they are as of `performance_as_of` (month-end), not `as_of_date` — the two date columns are easy to conflate.
State the row count (~116) and the advisory primary key `[ticker]`, and mention that Global X publishes no ISIN/CUSIP, so `ticker` is the only join key available.
7494bf5bb8f74a7b.summary: Column-level units are exemplary; the net-expense null rule is subtly wrong and null-heavy return columns go unmentioned.

suggestions: The docs say "prefer the `holdings` table" but never say why the scan exists or when it is actually the right call — one clause ("exposed because the extension needs a listed scan to discover filter pushdown; there is no query it answers that the table cannot") would stop an agent from hunting for a hidden capability.

The scan repeats the `fund_ticker`/`ticker` distinction and the percent-points note but omits the output columns entirely — an agent choosing between scan and table cannot see they are the same nine columns. State that it returns the `holdings` table's schema.

Clarify precedence when both the argument and a pushed `WHERE fund_ticker` predicate are present (the code unions them); as written, an agent may assume the argument wins and write `holdings_scan(fund_ticker => 'QYLD') WHERE fund_ticker = 'COPX'` expecting an empty result.
e5b8115a961743bb.summary: Argument semantics are documented accurately, but the scan hides its column list and never justifies its own existence.
